summary: This unit teaches you the everyday mathematics of a villa or hotel: whole numbers, fractions, decimals and percentages, metric units and conversions, ratio and scaling recipes, measuring and costing, money and exchange rates, time, and averages. You will learn to work out portions, orders, cleaning solutions, bills and areas, to estimate and check your answers, and to show your working clearly.

blocks.p: Mathematics is part of every job in a villa or hotel. The cook scales a recipe, the room attendant mixes cleaning solution, the front desk agent writes a bill and gives change, the pool attendant works out how much water a pool holds, and the supervisor works out how many staff the roster needs. A wrong answer costs money, wastes food or upsets a guest. This unit is for HOSPITALITY VILLA/PROPERTIES SERVICES LEVEL 2 trainees, and the same skills help you in any trade.

You will use a calculator, but you must still **understand what you are doing**. A calculator gives the answer to the numbers you press, not the answer to the job. That is why this unit also teaches you to estimate and to check.

Pick out the numbers and the units

blocks.note: How you are assessed: theory papers (multiple-choice, short answers and essays) and group practical tasks. In the practical tasks you measure a room and work out cleaning solution and cost, and you scale and make a fruit punch and cost it. The assessor checks your measuring, your working and your checking, not only the answers.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.note: Always write the unit with the answer (kg, ml, m², J$, hours). '5' may mean 5 kg or 5 g, and the difference matters.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: Whole numbers, order of operations and checking

blocks.p: For long sums, line up the digits by place value (units under units, tens under tens). Take care with zeros. Money in J$ often has thousands: write J$12 000 or J$12,000 as the property does.
When a calculation has more than one operation, do them in the right order or the answer will be wrong. **BODMAS** gives the order.

head: Calculation
Working
Answer
rows: Multiply first: J$3 000; then add J$900

blocks.note: On a bill, 2 dinners at J$3 000 each and 1 dessert at J$800 is 2 × 3 000 + 800 = J$6 800. If you add first (3 000 + 800) and then multiply by 2, you get J$7 600, which overcharges the guest. Most phone and scientific calculators follow BODMAS, but simple ones do not. Enter long calculations step by step.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: To **estimate**, round each number to an easy number (to the nearest 10, 100 or 1 000) and work the sum in your head. If your calculator answer is far from the estimate, you made a mistake.

head: Job
Estimate
Calculator answer
Verdict
rows: 48 guests × J$2 100 a head (wrong key press)

ul: **Estimate first**, then compare.
**Work backwards** with the opposite operation. If 5 000 − 3 650 = 1 350, check that 3 650 + 1 350 = 5 000.
**Do the sum again** a different way, or ask a co-worker to check it.
Check that all amounts are in the **same unit** and the **same currency**, and that the decimal point is in the right place.
Check chemical mixes and recipe amounts again before you pour or weigh.

blocks.note: Accuracy matters because a wrong bill upsets guests and loses trust, wrong change is a loss to the till, a wrong recipe wastes food, and a wrong chemical mix can damage surfaces or harm people.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: A **fraction** shows part of a whole. The bottom number (denominator) says how many equal parts the whole is cut into. The top number (numerator) says how many parts you have. A rum cake cut into 12 equal slices, with 8 eaten, has 8/12 eaten and 4/12 left. Both simplify: 8/12 = 2/3 and 4/12 = 1/3.

head: Job
How to do it
Example
rows: Divide top and bottom by the same number
Divide by the bottom, multiply by the top
Make the bottoms the same first
Divide by the number of parts
A 1.5 kg block cut into 3 equal pieces: 1.5 ÷ 3 = 0.5 kg = 500 g

blocks.p: A **decimal** uses a point to show parts of one. The digits after the point are tenths, hundredths, thousandths. 1.25 kg is one kilogram and 25 hundredths of a kilogram. To change a fraction into a decimal, divide the top by the bottom: 3/8 = 3 ÷ 8 = 0.375.

ul: To add or subtract decimals, line up the decimal points. 1.25 kg + 0.75 kg = 2.00 kg.
To multiply by 10, 100 or 1 000, move the point right by 1, 2 or 3 places. To divide, move it left.
To multiply money: 4 bottles at J$185.50 = 4 × 185.50 = J$742.00.

blocks.p: **Rounding** makes a number simpler. Look at the digit just after the place you are rounding to. If it is 5 or more, round up. If it is 4 or less, leave it.

head: Number
Round to
Answer
rows: 3.5 kg (7 is 5 or more, so up)

blocks.note: When you **order** goods, round **up** to whole packs or bags. If you need 9.9 kg and rice comes in 2 kg bags, 9.9 ÷ 2 = 4.95, so you buy 5 bags. Rounding down would leave you short. For money in J$, round to the nearest cent as the property does, or to the nearest dollar if the property says so.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: Jamaica uses the metric system (kilograms, litres, metres). Older recipes, markets and some equipment use pounds, ounces and degrees Fahrenheit. A good worker can change between them.

flow: Find the unit you have and the unit you need
Bigger to smaller: multiply (by 10, 100 or 1 000)
Smaller to bigger: divide
Write the new unit beside the answer

blocks.note: Put all the amounts in the **same unit** before you add them or scale them. Mixing grams and kilograms in one sum is a common mistake.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: Many Jamaican markets and suppliers still sell by the pound. As a guide, **1 kg is about 2.2 lb**, and **1 lb is about 454 g**. If yam costs J$280 a pound, one kilogram costs about 2.2 × 280 = J$616. Always check which unit the price is for.

blocks.note: Markets and suppliers in Jamaica often quote prices per pound while recipes use grams and kilograms. Convert before you compare prices or cost a recipe.
blocks.label: Jamaica

head: Change
Rule
Example
rows: 350 °F: (350 − 32) × 5/9 = 318 × 5/9 = about 177 °C. Ovens are set to about 180 °C

blocks.p: Useful food safety temperatures are given in the food safety plan and should be learned there. For example, cold food is kept at 5 °C or below.
The front desk gets a rate each day: how many Jamaican dollars equal US$1. Use the rate the property gives for the day.

blocks.note: Guests can pay in US$ or J$. If the rate is not given, ask your supervisor. Never guess or use yesterday's rate.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: **Per cent** means 'out of 100'. 25% is 25 out of 100, which is 25/100 = 1/4 = 0.25. Hotels use percentages for service charges, taxes, discounts, occupancy and food cost.

blocks.h: Finding a percentage of an amount

flow: Change the percentage to a decimal: divide by 100
Multiply by the amount

blocks.p: A quick way to find **10%** is to divide by 10. **5%** is half of 10%. **1%** is dividing by 100. To find 15%, add 10% and 5%.

blocks.h: Adding or taking away a percentage

head: Job
Method 1
Method 2 (one step)
rows: Add a 10% service charge to J$7 500
Add a tax at the 'current rate'
Work out the rate as a percentage and add it

blocks.note: GCT (general consumption tax) and other taxes are added in the same way as a service charge, using the **current rate** that the property or the tax authority gives. Never use a rate from memory.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.note: When a discount and a charge are both used, check which amount each is calculated on. A 10% discount takes 10% off the original price. A 10% service charge added afterwards is 10% of the new, lower amount. They do not cancel out.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.h: What percentage is one number of another?

flow: Divide the part by the whole
Multiply by 100
Write the % sign

head: Job
Working
Answer
rows: Two staff are absent out of a team of 16

blocks.p: The **food cost percentage** shows how much of the selling price is spent on ingredients: cost of one portion ÷ selling price × 100.

flow: List every ingredient and the amount used
Cost each amount from the purchase price
Add them to find the cost of the recipe
Divide by the number of portions
Divide the cost of one portion by the selling price and multiply by 100

head: Item
Cost / price
rows: Ingredients for 4 plates of stew chicken

blocks.p: If the kitchen wants a food cost of 32% and a plate costs J$480 to make, the selling price should be 480 ÷ 0.32 = J$1 500. Kitchens compare their results with their target and change prices or portions if needed.

blocks.note: A rise in the cost of one ingredient, such as chicken, raises the food cost percentage unless the price or the portion changes. That is why kitchens re-cost their dishes regularly.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: Ratio, proportion, scaling recipes and yield

blocks.p: A **ratio** compares amounts. A ratio of 1 : 9 means 1 part of the first thing to 9 parts of the second. You can write it in its simplest form by dividing both numbers by the same number: 12 : 18 = 2 : 3.

flow: Add the parts to get the total number of parts
Divide the amount you need by the total parts: this is one part
Multiply one part by each number in the ratio
Check: the amounts add up to the total

head: Job
Working
rows: 500 ml of cleaning solution, concentrate : water = 1 : 4
1 + 4 = 5 parts; 500 ÷ 5 = 100 ml per part; concentrate 100 ml, water 400 ml; check 100 + 400 = 500 ml
1 + 9 = 10 parts; 1 000 ÷ 10 = 100 ml concentrate and 900 ml water
A punch: 2 parts juice to 1 part soda, with 4 L of juice
4 L is 2 parts, so 1 part is 2 L; soda = 2 L

blocks.note: The ratio is for the **parts**, not for the amount of water you add to a whole bottle. 1 : 9 means 1 part concentrate **to** 9 parts water, and the mix is 10 parts in all. Always use the ratio on the maker's label and measure with a marked jug.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.p: In **direct proportion**, if one amount doubles, so does the other. The unitary method works well: find the amount for one, then multiply.

head: Job
Working
rows: 5 kg of potatoes cost J$1 250. What do 8 kg cost?
A recipe for 4 people uses 300 g of rice. How much for 10 people?

blocks.p: In **inverse proportion**, if one amount goes up, the other goes down. If two room attendants take 6 hours to clean a villa, three attendants working at the same rate take 2 × 6 ÷ 3 = 4 hours. More workers means less time.

flow: Find the conversion factor: new portions ÷ old portions
Multiply every ingredient by the factor
Write the new amounts on a new recipe card
Check tin sizes, cooking time and seasoning

blocks.p: To scale **down**, the factor is less than 1. A recipe for 12 cut to 3 has a factor of 3 ÷ 12 = 0.25. Strong flavours such as spices and salt may need less than the exact factor, so taste and adjust as the recipe allows. Baking times may change with the size of the tin.

**Yield** is how much usable food you get. Peeling, trimming and bones make waste, so you must buy more than you serve. **AP** is the 'as purchased' weight and **EP** is the 'edible portion' after waste.

head: Job
Working
Answer
rows: A 2 kg chicken loses 30% in bones and trimming. Usable meat?
A pot holds 4.5 kg of rice and peas. Each portion is 150 g. Portions?
Yield percentage if 5 kg of yam gives 4 kg after peeling

flow: Find the number of guests and the portion size
Multiply: portion × guests = total amount
Add a margin for waste and second helpings (often about 10%, or as the kitchen's policy says)
Check what is already in the store room
Round up to the pack sizes the supplier sells

blocks.p: Example: a function for 60 guests with 150 g of rice each needs 60 × 150 = 9 000 g = 9 kg. Adding 10% (0.9 kg) gives 9.9 kg. Rice comes in 2 kg bags: 9.9 ÷ 2 = 4.95, so order 5 bags (10 kg).

sections.title: Measuring: perimeter, area, volume and circles

ul: Hold the tape straight and tight, with the end hooked on the edge or held firmly on the mark.
Read at eye level and write the measurement down at once, with its unit.
Have a second person read the tape to check.
Measure in the same unit (mm or m). Change millimetres to metres by dividing by 1 000.
Make a simple labelled sketch before you calculate.

blocks.note: Do not let a steel tape snap back: the edge can cut. Do not stand on a chair or bed to measure.
blocks.label: Safety

head: Shape
Perimeter (around the edge)
Area (the flat space inside)
rows: Rectangle, length L and width W
Triangle, base B and height H

head: Job
Working
Answer
rows: Buffet table 2.4 m by 0.8 m: skirting round the four sides
A bedroom floor 5 m by 4 m
A triangular flower bed with base 6 m and height 4 m
A square tile 300 mm each side, in m²

blocks.note: Area is always in **square** units (m², cm²). Perimeter is in ordinary units (m, cm). If a room has a fixed part that is not cleaned (a built-in wardrobe), find its area and **subtract** it from the floor area.
blocks.label: Remember

head: Job
Working
Answer
rows: Floor 6.4 m by 3.5 m with a fixed counter 1.6 m by 0.6 m
One litre of polish covers 40 m². Lobby of 120 m²

blocks.p: **Volume** is the space inside a solid. For a box shape (a rectangular tank or pool) it is length × width × depth. Volume in m³ can be changed to litres: 1 m³ = 1 000 L.

head: Job
Working
Answer
rows: A pool 3 m long, 2 m wide and 1 m deep
A water tank 2 m by 1.5 m by 1.2 m

blocks.note: Many villas in Jamaica store water in tanks because the supply is not always steady. Knowing how many litres a tank holds helps you plan use and fill times.
blocks.label: Jamaica

head: Word
Meaning
rows: The distance straight across the circle through the centre
The distance from the centre to the edge: half the diameter
The distance round the edge: C = π × d

blocks.p: **π (pi)** is about 3.14 (correct to two decimal places). Example: a round cake 20 cm across needs a ribbon of 3.14 × 20 = 62.8 cm, which is about 63 cm. A round table with a radius of 0.75 m has an area of 3.14 × 0.75 × 0.75 = 1.77 m² (to 2 decimal places).

blocks.note: A common mistake is to use the **diameter** in the area formula instead of the radius. Halve the diameter first.
blocks.label: Tip

flow: List each item with its price and quantity
Multiply price × quantity for each line
Add the lines to get the subtotal
Take off any discount
Add any service charge and tax
State the total and the currency
Take payment and give change

head: Example bill
Working
rows: 2 club sandwiches at J$1 800 and 3 juices at J$650
Bar bill J$3 650 paid with a J$5 000 note
Dinner bill J$12 000 plus 10% service charge

blocks.note: Count change back to the guest, starting from the bill amount and working up to the note they gave you. This is the way to check it as you give it. Always keep the cash in the till until the sale is done.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: Time is not in tens. There are **60 minutes in an hour**, not 100. Add hours and minutes separately and carry when minutes reach 60.

head: Job
Working
Answer
rows: Reception starts at 19:30 and lasts 2 h 45 min
A room attendant starts at 08:00; villa 1 takes 1 h 45, villa 2 takes 2 h 30, then a 30-min break

blocks.note: The number of **nights** is check-out date minus check-in date, not the number of days named. A guest who checks in on the 12th and out on the 17th stays 5 nights.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: **24-hour time** counts 00:00 to 23:59, so 18:45 is 6:45 p.m. in 12-hour time. To change, subtract 12 from the hours after 12:59.
The **mean** (or average) is the total divided by the number of values. The **median** is the middle value when they are in order. The **range** is the highest minus the lowest.
Managers use averages to plan: the average number of breakfasts a day helps them decide how much to order and how many staff to roster.

blocks.h: Reading tables, menus and price lists

ul: Read the heading of each column and row first.
Check the unit (per kg, per lb, per night) and the currency.
Take the amount from the right row and column.
Multiply price × quantity for each line before you add.

blocks.note: Show your working in every calculation: write the figures, the operation and the unit on each line. If you make a mistake, a clear line of working lets you or a co-worker find it. In an assessment, working earns marks even when the final answer has a slip.
blocks.label: Tip

c1.title: A wedding at a Negril villa
c1.text: A villa in Negril is catering for a wedding lunch for 80 guests. The kitchen plans 220 g of raw chicken for each guest. Chicken is bought in 2.5 kg boxes. The jerk sauce recipe on the card makes enough for 8 portions and uses 240 ml of sauce base. The ingredients for one plate cost J$1 350.

c2.title: Cleaning a villa lounge in Port Antonio
c2.text: Room attendant Janelle measures a villa lounge with a tape. The length reads 6 400 mm and the width 3 500 mm. A fixed bar counter that is not cleaned takes up 1.6 m by 0.6 m of the floor. She mixes floor cleaner 1 part concentrate to 19 parts water, and she needs 5 L of the mixed solution. The concentrate costs J$3 200 for a 5 L container.

c3.title: A guest bill at the front desk
c3.text: Mr. Peter Ellis checks in at a villa on 14 July and checks out on 19 July. The room rate is US$180 a night. He gets a 10% discount on the room charge for a long stay, and then a 10% service charge is added to the discounted amount. The front desk rate for the day is J$155 for US$1. Mr. Ellis pays the whole bill in J$ with J$140 000 in cash.

c4.title: Fruit punch for a pool party
c4.text: The bar at a villa in Ocho Rios makes 7.5 L of fruit punch for a pool party, mixed 3 parts juice to 2 parts soda water. The punch is served in 200 ml glasses from a 1.8 L jug. A batch of 40 glasses costs J$3 000 in ingredients, and each glass is sold for J$300.

c5.title: The pool and garden at a Mandeville villa
c5.text: A villa in Mandeville has a rectangular pool 8 m long and 4 m wide, with an average depth of 1.5 m. A hose adds water at 40 litres per minute. In the garden there is a round flower bed 4 m across, which the gardener plans to edge with a rope. Use 3.14 for π.

questions.q: How much raw chicken does the kitchen need for 80 guests?
questions.why: 80 × 220 g = 17 600 g, and 17 600 ÷ 1 000 = 17.6 kg. Check by estimating: 80 × 200 g = 16 kg, so about 17 to 18 kg is right. The other answers have the decimal point in the wrong place or a slip in the sum.

questions.q: The chicken comes in 2.5 kg boxes. How many boxes should be ordered for 17.6 kg?
questions.why: 17.6 ÷ 2.5 = 7.04, and you cannot buy part of a box, so round up to 8. Seven boxes would be 17.5 kg, which is short. 44 is what you get by multiplying instead of dividing.

questions.q: How much jerk sauce base is needed for 80 portions?
questions.why: The factor is 80 ÷ 8 = 10, so 240 ml × 10 = 2 400 ml = 2.4 L. 19.2 L comes from 240 ml × 80, which forgets to divide by the 8 portions in the recipe.

questions.q: Chef Sheldon decides he wants the food cost of the plate to be 30% instead. What selling price does he need?
questions.why: Food cost % = cost ÷ price × 100, so price = cost ÷ 0.30 = 1 350 ÷ 0.30 = J$4 500. Check: 30% of 4 500 = 1 350. J$405 is 30% of the cost, and J$1 755 is the cost plus 30%.

questions.q: What is the length of the lounge in metres?
questions.why: There are 1 000 mm in 1 m, so 6 400 ÷ 1 000 = 6.4 m. A lounge 64 m long would be bigger than a football pitch, so the estimate also shows the others are wrong.

questions.q: How much floor does Janelle have to clean?
questions.why: Floor: 6.4 × 3.5 = 22.4 m². Counter: 1.6 × 0.6 = 0.96 m². Subtract: 22.4 − 0.96 = 21.44 m². 22.4 m² forgets to take away the counter, and 23.36 m² adds it.

questions.q: How much water is used to make the 5 L of solution, mixed 1 part concentrate to 19 parts water?
questions.why: 1 + 19 = 20 parts, and 5 000 ml ÷ 20 = 250 ml per part. Concentrate is 1 part = 250 ml, and water is 19 parts = 4 750 ml = 4.75 L. Check: 250 + 4 750 = 5 000 ml. 19 L comes from treating each part as 1 L.

questions.q: About how much does the 250 ml of concentrate in each 5 L batch cost?
questions.why: A 5 L container is 5 000 ml. 250 ml is 1/20 of it, so J$3 200 ÷ 20 = J$160. J$320 would be 1/10 of the container.

questions.q: How many nights does Mr. Ellis stay?
questions.why: Nights are the check-out date minus the check-in date: 19 − 14 = 5. Counting both dates would give 6, which is an overcharge.

questions.q: What is Mr. Ellis's bill in US$, with the discount and then the service charge?
questions.why: Five nights at US$180 = US$900. The 10% discount is US$90, leaving US$810. The 10% service charge on US$810 is US$81, so the total is US$891. US$900 comes from taking off and adding 10% of the same amount, as if they cancelled; US$810 forgets the service charge.

questions.q: How much is the bill of US$891 in Jamaican dollars?
questions.why: US$ to J$ is multiplied by the rate: 891 × 155 = J$138 105. J$5.75 comes from dividing instead, and that answer is far too small to be sensible, since J$ amounts are always much bigger than US$ amounts.

questions.q: How much change must the cashier give Mr. Ellis?
questions.why: 140 000 − 138 105 = J$1 895. Check by adding up: 138 105 + 1 895 = 140 000. The other answers have an error in one digit when subtracting.

questions.q: How many full 200 ml glasses can be filled from one 1.8 L jug?
questions.why: 1.8 L = 1 800 ml, and 1 800 ÷ 200 = 9. Always put both amounts in the same unit first. 90 comes from forgetting to change litres into millilitres properly.

questions.q: In 7.5 L of punch mixed 3 parts juice to 2 parts soda, how much juice is needed?
questions.why: 3 + 2 = 5 parts, so one part is 7.5 ÷ 5 = 1.5 L. Juice is 3 × 1.5 = 4.5 L and soda is 2 × 1.5 = 3 L. Check: 4.5 + 3 = 7.5 L. 3 L is the amount of soda.

questions.q: What percentage of the selling price of one glass is the cost of ingredients?
questions.why: One glass costs 3 000 ÷ 40 = J$75. Then 75 ÷ 300 × 100 = 25%. 75% is the part of the price left over as profit, and 400% comes from dividing the price by the cost.

questions.q: How many litres of water does the pool hold when it is full?
questions.why: Volume = 8 × 4 × 1.5 = 48 m³, and 1 m³ = 1 000 L, so the pool holds 48 000 L. 13 500 comes from adding the three measurements instead of multiplying.

questions.q: How long will the hose take to fill the empty pool at 40 litres per minute?
questions.why: 48 000 ÷ 40 = 1 200 minutes, and 1 200 ÷ 60 = 20 hours. 1 200 hours forgets to change minutes into hours.

questions.q: What is the area of the round flower bed?
questions.why: The radius is half of 4 m = 2 m. Area = 3.14 × 2 × 2 = 12.56 m². 50.24 m² comes from using the diameter (4 m) in place of the radius.

questions.q: Occupied rooms in a hotel from Monday to Friday were 34, 41, 38, 47 and 50. What was the mean number of rooms occupied per day?
questions.why: Total = 34 + 41 + 38 + 47 + 50 = 210, and 210 ÷ 5 = 42. 41 is the median (the middle number when in order), 210 is the total and 16 is the range.

questions.q: A breakfast cook starts at 06:45 and finishes at 15:15, with a 45-minute unpaid break. How long does the cook work?
questions.why: 06:45 to 15:15 is 8 hours 30 minutes. Take off the 45-minute break: 8 h 30 min − 45 min = 7 h 45 min. 8 hours 30 minutes forgets the break.
